summary: due date is what the Credit card payment calculator works out, and it gets there from the credit card balance, the interest rate APR, the desired payoff date and the payback within. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Credit card payment calculator work?
sections.html:
The Credit card payment calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports due date in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the minimum percentage type and the compounding frequency); then you give the desired payoff date; then you type in the credit card balance, the interest rate APR, the payback within and the minimum percentage.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

3 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Credit card payment calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Due date=desired payoff date − 1461 ÷ 2
Payoff date=((((monthly payment with..., credit card balance, due date, interest rate APR, desired payoff date, payback within, minimum percentage type, minimum percentage, minimum payment, compounding frequency)))) + 1

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent
  • Time, opening in years / months

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Credit card payment calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the credit card balance, the interest rate APR and the desired payoff date — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Credit card payment calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns due date, derived from the credit card balance, the interest rate APR and the desired payoff date. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Credit card payment calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the credit card balance, the interest rate APR, the desired payoff date and the payback within, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter credit card balance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Credit card balance opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Credit card payment calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
